title: dBm and Milliwatts: RF Power the Log Way
h1: dBm and mW — decibel-milliwatts across radio links
description: Radio engineers speak in dBm. A 20 dBm signal is 100 mW. Here is the log math and why every WiFi and cellular signal ends up expressed this way.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review

hero: A 20 dB path loss cuts your signal by 100×. Adding losses in dB is just adding numbers. That is why RF engineers never went back to linear power.
body: Radio signals span 15 orders of magnitude from transmitter (watts) to receiver (femtowatts). Linear units get unreadable. The decibel-milliwatt (dBm) compresses that range into a comfortable ±100 window and turns cascaded loss calculations into addition.

> P(dBm) = 10 × log₁₀(P/1 mW)
> 0 dBm = 1 mW
> +10 dBm = 10 mW
> +20 dBm = 100 mW
> +30 dBm = 1 W
> −30 dBm = 1 µW
> −60 dBm = 1 nW
> −90 dBm = 1 pW

A link budget adds transmitter power, subtracts path loss, adds antenna gain, subtracts cable loss. In linear terms these are multiplications. In dB they are additions. A 100-page cellular design document works in dB throughout because signed arithmetic beats scientific notation every time.

WiFi transmit power: +20 dBm = 100 mW. Cell phone tx: +23 dBm = 200 mW. WiFi receiver sensitivity: −80 dBm = 10 pW. LTE minimum received power: −120 dBm = 1 fW. Bluetooth Class 2: +4 dBm = 2.5 mW. FM broadcast transmitter: +90 dBm = 1 MW.
## Worked example — a WiFi link budget

Router transmits at +20 dBm (100 mW). Router antenna gain: +3 dBi. Free-space path loss at 5 m, 2.4 GHz: ~54 dB. Two walls: −10 dB. Client antenna: +0 dBi. Client sensitivity: −72 dBm. Received power = 20 + 3 − 54 − 10 + 0 = −41 dBm. Margin above sensitivity: 31 dB — comfortable. At 20 m with 4 walls: 20 + 3 − 66 − 20 = −63 dBm, margin 9 dB — marginal, packet loss likely.
## dBi, dBd, dBc — the other decibels

dBi = gain relative to isotropic radiator. dBd = gain relative to dipole (add 2.15 dB for dBi). dBc = level relative to a carrier. Always read the suffix — a '10 dB antenna' with no suffix is ambiguous.
0 dBm = 1 mW. Each +10 dB = 10× power. Each +3 dB ≈ 2×. Add dB values through a link; don't multiply linear watts.

faqs.q: Why is dB always divided by 10?
faqs.a: Because a bel is 10 dB. The bel was a large unit; the deci-bel is more useful for everyday electronics. The name honours Alexander Graham Bell.

faqs.q: Is dBm the same as dB?
faqs.a: No. dB is dimensionless (a ratio). dBm is dB referenced to 1 mW — an absolute power. Similarly dBW is referenced to 1 W (0 dBW = 30 dBm).

faqs.q: What is a good WiFi RSSI?
faqs.a: Above −60 dBm: excellent. −60 to −70: good. −70 to −80: fair. Below −80: unreliable. Below −90: no connection.
